facts.headline: A temple's shimmering spire is built from literal trash
facts.body_html: Wat Arun's 70-meter spire is covered in millions of pieces of broken Chinese porcelain — plates and bowls used as ballast on trading ships and discarded once they reached port. Craftsmen pressed the shards into intricate floral patterns, and they still hand-repair the mosaic today.

Wat Arun Temple of Dawn Chao Phraya river

facts.headline: A king turned this temple's walls into Thailand's first encyclopedia
facts.body_html: In the 1830s, King Rama III had Wat Pho's walls inscribed with everything from medicine to astrology — reasoning that books burn but stone doesn't. The complex is also the birthplace of traditional Thai massage, still taught there today.
suggested_queries: Wat Pho reclining Buddha temple exterior

facts.headline: Only one person on Earth is allowed to touch this statue — and only 3 times a year
facts.body_html: Thailand's most sacred object, the Emerald Buddha, gets its cloak changed by the king himself for each season — cool, hot, and rainy. No one else is permitted to touch it, and despite the name, it isn't actually made of emerald.
suggested_queries: Grand Palace Bangkok Wat Phra Kaew exterior
Temple of the Emerald Buddha Bangkok facade

facts.headline: This city's real name has 168 characters — and holds a world record
facts.body_html: Bangkok's full ceremonial name, Krung Thep Mahanakhon..., runs 168 characters and is recognized by Guinness as the longest place name on Earth. Locals almost never use it; the English name actually comes from an old village called 'place of hog plums.'

facts.headline: Parts of this city are only half a meter above sea level — and dropping
facts.body_html: Built on soft clay, Bangkok has been sinking for decades, driven mostly by groundwater extraction. It was sinking up to 10 centimeters a year in the 1970s before pumping bans slowed it — but some districts are still dropping today.

facts.headline: More than 200,000 people pass through this market in a single weekend
facts.body_html: Chatuchak spans roughly 35 acres and packs thousands of stalls into 27 sections, making it one of the largest markets on the planet. It started as a 1940s government plan to put one market in every province.

facts.headline: This city used to be crossed by canals instead of roads
facts.body_html: 19th-century visitors called Bangkok the 'Venice of the East' — in 1855, three-quarters of its population lived on boats or stilted houses along the khlongs. Most canals were later paved over, but floating markets still run on the ones that remain.
